Description: Software engineering is the branch of computer science that addresses the organisation of and the methods, tools and techniques used in the whole software lifecycle: how do we get from an idea for some IT support to a piece of software used by the intended beneficiaries. Modern software products is not developed by individual programmers, but by teams, sometimes very large teams. Collaboration both within the team and with intended users is therefore at the core of software engineering. The course introduces to professional software engineering, enabling the student to competently act as a project member and to take over management responsibility for minor projects. Special emphasis is put on how the organisation of the development process influences software product qualities and the software quality-in-use. The course combines introduction to central themes in software engineering. Specifically, it introduces into: a process based perspective on software engineeringdifferent ways of organizing the software engineering (development models)supporting process areas, such as project management, configuration management, quality management, and process improvementobject oriented analysis and design leading up to requirements specification and architectural design. different quality dimensions, such as software use qualities, software product qualities, software process qualities and how to address them Note that there will be NO coding activities in the course.
Exam: D: Submission of written work with following oral, External (7-point scale)

Course Summary: New mandatory course for BDDIT 2024 The course Software and AI studies provides students with an introduction to the basic theoretical, practical, and critical principles of artificial intelligence and its social and cultural impacts. After the course, the student will understand how various AI systems—including classification models, deep learning networks, language models, and generative systems—operate within modern software ecosystems. The student will be able to use, adapt, and evaluate basic AI applications through guided exercises with existing tools and frameworks, gaining hands-on experience with model configuration, data preparation, and performance evaluation. The course furthermore introduces the students to critical readings of AI, to provide the student with necessary perspectives to understand the societal, ethical, and cultural implications of AI-powered software systems.

Description: New mandatory course for BDDIT 2024 AI is increasingly integrated into software systems across various domains, including government, healthcare, and consumer products. These systems are inherently complex, relying on large curated datasets, extensive computational training, and integration within intricate software architectures. This course provides students with an introduction to AI systems within digital design. Additionally, students will develop the skills to critically evaluate the potential negative implications and societal impacts of machine learning systems. The course is organized across three complementary dimensions: TheoreticalStudents will acquire the vocabulary necessary to understand the foundational aspects of AI systems. Students will learn to differentiate between various AI approaches that are increasingly embedded in human-facing applications, including classification systems, deep learning architectures, natural language processing, large language models, and generative systems, becoming familiar with their fundamental principles and capabilities, and societal and ethical implications. PracticalStudents will work with existing frameworks to configure, train, and evaluate AI models through guided exercises. They will gain hands-on experience with image classification, bias detection, language processing, and generative systems, learning how technical choices influence the behavior and limitations of user-facing AI applications. CriticalStudents will engage with contemporary critiques of AI through reading and discussion, reflecting on the potential misuse and societal risks associated with these technologies. They will learn to assess the negative consequences of machine learning systems and critically analyze their ethical implications.Use of generative artificial intelligence is allowed with restrictions during the exam (see LearnIT), as long as the student follows the official ITU guidelines on generative artificial intelligence.

Description: New Special Topic / Specialisation course for KDDIT 2024 Interaction design is the discipline where humans and computers meet. It frames how we interact with an increasingly digitalized world, as well as how we relate to one another. This course imagines and creates new forms of interaction and applications for computing based on a particular topic each semester. It uses a combination of methods, materials, and mediums from HCI, design, and art to develop new things that make arguments or claims about how things might be done differently, with an eye towards producing preferable futures. This course will cover interaction design methods and theory through both in-class examples as well as a design project in groups. Over the course of the semester, groups will develop an interactive artefact or set artefacts in response to a design brief they produce. This design process will be informed by research that roots the brief in a particular situation and context, with a particular audience in mind. Students will have the opportunity to engage in a complete design process from requirements gathering through to prototyping, while developing methodological and theoretical capacities to express intentionality as part of a practice based in use, societal context, and/or art. All use of generative artificial intelligence is allowed during the exam, as long as the student follows the official ITU guidelines on generative artificial intelligence.
Exam: D: Submission of written work with following oral, External (7-point scale)

Description: New Special Topic / Specialisation for KDDIT 2024 For UX designers, the ability to adapt to new technological developments and changing societal demands is crucial. From ChatGPT to self-driving cars, AI-driven products have become increasingly integrated into many aspects of industries as well as our daily lives. What is the new design space opened up by this new technology? How do designers effectively work with these highly technical systems? And how do designers place human values (such as trust, agency, and ethics) in the center of AI/Machine Learning? The course emphasizes how to engage emergent technology, such as AI, Machine learning, and Generative AI, as a design material. In addition to established UX design theories and methods, the course will cover advanced topics in human-AI interaction. Students will develop expertise in designing the UX of AI-driven products. They will gain hands-on experience in data-driven user research, prototyping AI interactions, and applying UX design methodologies tailored to AI-driven experiences. All use of generative artificial intelligence is allowed during the exam, as long as the student follows the official ITU guidelines on generative artificial intelligence.

Course Summary: Kurset giver den studerende kompetencer til at analysere og reflektere over styringen af it-projekter i en kompleks organisatorisk kontekst. Det sker gennem arbejdet med en række temaer hvor vi afdækker, og reflekterer teoretisk over, centrale forhold og problemfelter inden for feltet.
Abstract: Kurset giver den studerende kompetencer til at analysere og reflektere over styringen af it-projekter i en kompleks organisatorisk kontekst. Det sker gennem arbejdet med en række temaer hvor vi afdækker, og reflekterer teoretisk over, centrale forhold og problemfelter inden for feltet.
Description: Organisering og ledelse af digitaliseringsprojekter er vigtigt for de fleste organisationer både i den private og offentlige sektor. Projekterne designes, planlægges, udvikles og implementeres i organisatoriske kontekster hvor de konkurrerer om mål, opmærksomhed og ressourcer med andre projekter og den daglige drift. Projekterne lever i et landskab med mange forskellige til dels modsatrettede interesser, og en dynamisk og delvist uforudsigelig omverden. Det er i disse komplekse omgivelser projektlederen skal sikre at projektet lykkes og bidrager il at virksomheden kan opfylde sine mål. Dette kursus dækker både metoder fra praksis og indsigt fra forskning, med vægt på forskning. Deltagerne får kendskab til de metoder der anvendes i digitaliseringsprojekter og viden om den organisatoriske virkelighed projekterne lever i. Deltagerne diskuterer, relateret til forskningen indenfor området, styrker og mangler ved forskellige tilgange. Desuden vil deltagerne lære at anvende viden og koncepter fra forskningen til at forstå og håndtere udfordringerne i styringen af digitaliseringsprojekter. Hvor mainstream fremstillinger af bæredygtighed ofte er et spørgsmål om teknologisk innovation, tilgår kurset bæredygtighed som sustain-abilities: evnen til at handle, tage ansvar, drage omsorg, og navigere i komplekse sociale, teknologiske og økologiske relationer. Description: Kurset introducerer de studerende til bæredygtighed som en situeret, omstridt og relationel praksis. Hvor mainstream fremstillinger af bæredygtighed ofte er et spørgsmål om teknologisk innovation, tilgår kurset bæredygtighed som sustain-abilities: evnen til at handle, tage ansvar, drage omsorg, og navigere i komplekse sociale, teknologiske og økologiske relationer. De studerende undersøger og diskuterer dominerende antagelser om bæredygtighed, herunder hvordan begreber som “den grønne omstilling” forstås i sociotekniske sammenhænge. Et centralt element i kurset er studenterdrevet, casebaseret arbejde, hvor de studerende gennem kurset arbejder med en selvvalgt socioteknisk situation. Dette giver mulighed for at udforske og praktisere egne sustain-abilities i konkrete og situerede sammenhænge og understøtter de studerendes evne til at handle i komplekse situationer præget af modstridende værdier og ufuldstændig viden. Course Summary: This course guides students in contextualizing, analyzing, critiquing, and reflecting upon the role of IT in enacting more sustainable futures. While digital technologies are seen as a means of mitigating climate effects and buttressing sustainability practices, they are also complex planetary assemblages that require vast quantities of resources to design, build, and implement. In this course, students will engage with a wide variety of readings to develop their understanding of various perspectives on Sustainable IT. As part of the course, students get the opportunity to select a suitable Sustainable IT case to work with, develop a synopsis (in groups), and analyze their given case using one of the perspectives offered in the course (material-infrastructural, organizational, interventionist, governance, planetary).

Description: This course guides students in contextualizing, analyzing, critiquing, and reflecting upon the role of IT in enacting more sustainable futures. Digital Technologies (and the IT industry more generally) are playing an increasingly important role in the Climate Emergency. On one hand, these technologies are seen as a means of mitigating climate effects (reducing carbon impacts, enhancing sustainability practices). On the other, they are complex planetary assemblages that require vast quantities of resources to design, build, and implement, while simultaneously enabling forms of living that are less conducive to sustainable futures (24/7 internet, consumerism). This course brings sustainable thinking and action into conversation with IT, exploring how digital technologies can be mobilized to enact more sustainable futures. Students will engage with a wide array of readings to develop their understanding of various perspectives on Sustainable IT. After an initial engagement with sustainability and IT as concepts, students will go on to study; 1) how IT is manifested materially (through its extractions, infrastructures, and wastes) as well as how it measures and quantifies sustainability claims. 2) how IT is deployed within organizations to tackle the challenges of sustainability. 3) how other societal actors (NGOs, industry organizations, supra state entities) are intervening and shaping debates around sustainability and IT. 4) how planetary thinking is implicated in IT practices, logics, and ideologies. As part of the course, students will select a suitable Sustainable IT case to work with, develop a synopsis (in groups), and analyze their given case using one of the perspectives offered in the course (material, infrastructural, organizational, governance, interventionist, planetary).

Course Summary: The goal of this course is to provide students with a broad understanding of the challenges involved in managing a software development project, as well as well-established techniques and tools available to address these challenges.
Abstract: The goal of this course is to provide students with a broad understanding of the challenges involved in managing a software development project, as well as well-established techniques and tools available to address these challenges.
Description: According to recent studies, IT project success rates internationally are very low, almost one third of them get cancelled and over half of them are challenged. Lack of skilled project management and executive support is stated as the main reason for failure. This course helps to address this problem in the industry by teaching the students taking the course the important skills of software project management. The goal of this course is to provide students with a broad understanding of the challenges involved in managing a software development project, as well as well-established techniques and tools available to address these challenges. This will allow students to act within a software development project either as team members or as project managers. The course includes a general introduction to IT project management and the methods and techniques used to manage an IT project. As a whole, the course provides an overview of different models and how they relate to IT project management. Content : Differences and similarities between different development models.Different ways to organize the development process, with particular focus on agile and plan-driven methods: waterfall Model and plan driven project management, and Scrum as the method for systems development and project management.Systems development and project management in multicultural and distributed teams.
Exam: D: Submission of written work with following oral, External (7-point scale)

Course Summary: Brugergrænsefladen er den del af et it-system man oplever og kan interagere med som bruger. Udvikling af software involverer design brugergrænseflader og deres primære elementer. Det er bl.a. skærmbilleder, knapper, links, video og lyd. Kurset giver et teoretisk og praktisk indblik i systematisk design og udvikling af brugergrænseflader.
Abstract: Brugergrænsefladen er den del af et it-system man oplever og kan interagere med som bruger. Udvikling af software involverer design brugergrænseflader og deres primære elementer. Det er bl.a. skærmbilleder, knapper, links, video og lyd. Kurset giver et teoretisk og praktisk indblik i systematisk design og udvikling af brugergrænseflader.
Description: Brugergrænserflader er central for for mange IT systemer og at kunne designe og udvikle dem systematisk er vigtigt for en software udvikler. Den studerende får i kurset et praktisk og teoretisk fundament for systematisk udvikling af brugergrænseflader. Målet med dette kursus er at gøre den studerende i stand til at designe brugergrænseflader på en systematisk måde samt vurdere user experience af en grænseflade herunder tage hensyn til brugerens behov, mål, den platform systemet skal køre på og de data systemet skal benytte. Kurset vil benytte sig af webprogrammering teknikker ( React/JavaScript), til at udvikling af konkrete brugergrænseflader. Detaljeret målbeskrivelse : Du skal kortfattet kunne beskrive brugerens arbejdsopgaver og arbejdssituation.Du skal kunne forklare, hvad brugervenlighed er og hvordan det kan måles.Du skal kunne forklare, hvordan kognitive forhold som gestalter og mentale modeller har indflydelse på brugerens opfattelse af et system.Du skal kunne designe og implementere en grænseflade systematisk ud fra en beskrivelse af arbejdsopgaverne og en datamodel.Du skal kunne udarbejde prototyper af brugergrænsefladen og vurdere hensigtsmæssigheden af forskellige slags prototyper i givne situationer.Du skal kunne teste brugervenligheden af en prototype, rapportere fundne problemer, og give forslag til forbedringer.
Exam: C: Submission of written work, External (7-point scale)

Course Name: TeachIT: Live radio and listening book - Engaging students in readings and group conversations
Course Summary: Location: 2F23/2F27, Emil Holms Kanal By presenting examples from own practice (teaching design ethnographic methods in qualitative research), Assistant Professor Stina Hasse Jørgensen will talk about experiences making live radio and listening books (in courses with many students enrolled). At the workshop, you will discuss how best to engage students in group conversations and readings via the live radio medium and make a small radio episode and a listening book connected to an article/topic you teach. The TeachIT will take place in the podcast studio at Emil Holms Kanal, and seats will be limited. Takeaways: * How to plan a live radio show * How to make a listening book with guiding questions * Engaging students in readings and discussions via other teaching formats Any questions? Contact Learning Support at learning@itu.dk or in 2D11, Rued Langgaards Vej.

It will focus on designing different forms of communication (writing, presenting orally, graphic design) correctly, effectively, and convincingly. There will be a theoretical introduction to the importance and principles of technical communication together with several individual and group based practical exercises.
Abstract: This course gives an introduction to technical communication. It will focus on designing different forms of communication (writing, presenting orally, graphic design) correctly, effectively, and convincingly. There will be a theoretical introduction to the importance and principles of technical communication together with several individual and group based practical exercises.
Description: Efficient and convincing communication will play a deciding role whether you get a job, a promotion, or whether you win a grant. Communication is also an integral part in technical jobs or in research: You will spend at least 20 percent of your time on communication, work in a team or lead a team yourself, or translate technical insights for a general audience or for management. In such a setting, poor communication can lead to major financial losses or even to serious catastrophes costing human lives. In this course the student will gain an understanding of why technical communication is important, and how technical information is communicated clearly, efficiently, and convincingly to a specific audience. In particular, the course will cover the following subjects: Challenges and failures of communication Importance and principles of technical communicationRhetoric principlesTeam-based communicationAudience analysis and subject researchCommunicating correctly, effectively, and convincinglyDesigning and delivering persuasive technical presentationsText design and reviewing, evaluating, testing documents and websitesSummarizing research findings, communication for web and social mediaTranslating research findings for a general audienceWriting definitions, documentation and instructionsWriting reports and proposalsWriting CVs and application materialsInformation design with figures, tables, and graphs
Exam: C: Submission of written work, Internal (7-point scale)

Course Summary: This course teaches the foundation of constructing user interfaces for computer systems. This problem is likely harder than you might think: computer program very often perform complex tasks, yet users demand and need simple interfaces. Producing such interfaces requires an understanding of both the user—e.g., what are they trying to accomplish? what do they know already?—and the computer system—e.g., how fast can we provide responses?
Abstract: This course teaches the foundation of constructing user interfaces for computer systems. Description: This course provides a high-level overview of the history and the essential concepts related to interaction design and the fundamental programming patterns commonly used in programming user interfaces. Course Summary: The course zooms in on the ongoing digital transformation of the Danish public sector and provides analytical and methodological tools for understanding and working with digitalization processes across governmental institutions and the private organisations that underpin their transformation.
Abstract: The course zooms in on the ongoing digital transformation of the Danish public sector and provides analytical and methodological tools for understanding and working with digitalization processes across governmental institutions and the private organisations that underpin their transformation.
Description: Public sectors are currently undergoing large-scale institutional changes, not least in Denmark, a world-leading IT nation. Digital technologies are transforming both internal work and management practices and the relation between welfare professionals and citizens. Understanding these processes of transformation and what they entail is crucial for working both in public sector with digitalization and e.g. as consultant in the private sector. This course provides theoretical tools and empirical insights into how public sector transformations take place and unfold in practice, with a focus on the Danish public sector. The course goes into depths with the 'how' of public sector digitalization: How are digitalization processes changing the landscapes and ecosystems of the public sector today, and which types of hopes, dreams and challenges are involved in these processes? The course consists of three main elements: Thematic focus: How are digitalisation processes changing and challenging the welfare state? How are local governmental institutions, welfare encounters, work, professions, and management practices changed by digitalization?Concepts and method: How do we study and make sense of the changing organisational practices of the Danish welfare state?Project work: Grouped in research teams, you will conduct ethnographic research projects in local governmental settings going through processes of digitalization. The course prepares and equips you to work at the forefront of public sector transformations. As part of the course, you will carry out your own group research project in a Danish governmental setting. Doing so, you will study the implementation and/or changes caused by digitalization, linking your empirical work to core theoretical concepts in the course. This project work will, furthermore, provide you with inspiration, method and theory reflections, empirical insights and analytical skills relevant for your master thesis as well as future employment.
Exam: D: Submission of written work with following oral, External (7-point scale)

The course will be divided into two main thematic parts: cyber threat intelligence, which focuses on methods for using information about past cyberattacks and known attacker groups, and empirical research in human factors in security, focusing on studying human behavior in security-critical systems. The course is aimed at students with a background in computer science/data science with basic knowledge of cybersecurity.

The course is aimed at students with a background in computer science/data science with basic knowledge of cybersecurity.
Description: Understanding relevant cyber threats, including methods used by attackers as well as behavior of legitimate users potentially leading to security-critical human errors is cruical in preventing, detecting and responding to cyberattacks. In this course, you will learn about how information about threats collected from a variety of sources can be used to improve protection of IT systems against cyberattacks. The course will focus on two areas which heavily rely on collecting and analysing data in cybersecurity context: 1) Cyber threat intelligence (CTI), working with data on cybersecurity threats based on past attacks or other intelligence sources. This part covers following topics: Analytical frameworks commonly used in CTI Principles and methods of intelligence Digital forensics and incident response Threat actors and attribution Specific emerging threats, such as AI or cyberwarfare 2) Human factors in cybersecurity, working on empirical research on human behavior in security-critical systems, causes of human errors and methods for their prevention. This part covers following topics: Research methods and ethics in human research User authentication Phishing and social engineering Use of generative AI during the exam:Use of generative artificial intelligence is allowed with restrictions during the exam (see LearnIT), as long as the student follows the official ITU guidelineson generative artificial intelligence.

Abstract: This course allows students to develop their knowledge of user experience (UX) design and research in the context of new-generation digital products, especially those infused with AI and machine learning technology (AI-infused products). This course presents a number of research-based approaches to user research and the iterative design of these intelligent digital products.
Description: As a digital designer, the ability to adapt to new technological developments and changing societal demands is crucial. AI-infused products are one of the fastest-growing areas in UX research and design today. From personalized services and virtual assistants to self-driving cars, these products have become increasingly integrated into many aspects of our life, with the promise to transform the way people work, live, and play. What is the new design space opened up by this new technology? How do designers effectively work with these highly technical systems? Above all, how do UX designers place human values (such as trust, agency, and ethics) in the center of AI? In this course, students will learn relevant design theories and UX methods and apply them to concept design and prototyping. While the course focuses on AI-infused products, no programming is required. The emphasis is on how to engage emergent technology, such as AI, as a design material. Students with a strong design background will learn how to adapt their design skills to the new context of AI-infused products. We also welcome students with technical backgrounds who are interested in users.

Course Summary: How do we design the user experience for products built on generative AI? Recent Machine Learning applications such as ChatGPT, DALL-E, and Midjourney showcase AI's potential to automatically generate high-quality texts and images. In this course, students will apply current human-AI interaction research and design methods to create UX for generative AI products. No programming background is required.
Abstract: How do we design the user experience for products built on generative AI? Recent Machine Learning applications such as ChatGPT, DALL-E, and Midjourney showcase AI's potential to automatically generate high-quality texts and images. In this course, students will apply current human-AI interaction research and design methods to create UX for generative AI products. No programming background is required.
Description: UX II aims to develop students' understanding and design skills for the new design material of AI/ML. It builds on the foundation of UX I, which focuses on "designing AI" and explores how to "design *with* AI." Through the design material of generative AI, the course will explore human-AI interaction design topics such as (co-)creativity, autonomy/agency, and ethics. For instance, what type of UX flow is appropriate for generative AI? What roles can users and AI each play when working together? What are the ethical implications when it is no longer easy to tell whether human professionals or AI created the given content? And how can designers help to foster a sustainable future ethically? In this course, students will practice UX design and evaluation methods and adapt them to the fast-growing area of generative AI. They will identify real-world use cases and apply Research through Design methods to explore contemporary issues at the forefront of UX design.
Exam: C: Submission of written work, External (7-point scale)

Course Summary: INDHOLD: Kurset introducerer deltagerne til teori, principper og praksis indenfor usability, med udgangspunkt i de fagområder usability traditionelt relaterer til: Human-computer Interaktion, interaktionsdesign, psykologi, human factors, Informationsarkitektur, målgruppeanalyse og etnografi. Dertil trækker kurset på emner fra områder som webdesign, softwareudvikling og projektledelse. Det gives som 14 ugers undervisning bestående af forelæsninger og øvelser . Øvelser foregår i grupper af 5-6 deltagere. De er primært praktisk udførelse af udvalgte metoder der kan relateres til usability, eksempelvis kortsortering, brugertest, ekspertvurdering, tilgængelighedstest, spørgeskemaundersøgelser, A/B-test og analyse af øjenbevægelser. Deltagerne forventes at bruge øvelsestid til praktisk udførelse og diskussion, mens der må forventes ekstra arbejdstid til de mindre skriftlige afleveringer der er knyttet til hver øvelse. Øvelsesrækken afsluttes med en samlet rapport, som de studerende fremlægger og diskuterer ved sidste forelæsning. TID: Onsdage 17:00 til 18:50 forelæsning i lokale 5A60. Øvelser efterfølgende.

Course Summary: This course will provide students with theoretical and analytical foundations that will allow them to analyze and understand how individuals and groups make use of contemporary digital technology in relation to their individual, organizational, or social contexts. Students will gain hands-on experience by analyzing specific use contexts and practices by working on concrete case studies.
Abstract: This course will provide students with theoretical and analytical foundations that will allow them to analyze and understand how individuals and groups make use of contemporary digital technology in relation to their individual, organizational, or social contexts. Students will gain hands-on experience by analyzing specific use contexts and practices by working on concrete case studies.
Description: During the course, students will be introduced to a broad understanding of the concept of context, as well as the methodological and analytical tools that will help to understand the everyday social and cultural contexts that affect how and whether users use digital products. During the course, students will be able to analyze and reflect on the personal, cultural and institutional forces that today influence the development and use of digital services and media products. This will be done through an introduction to, among other things, theories of why people use (digital) media, online cultural studies, current sociological theory with a focus on group formation and group identity, critical-oriented platform theory, as well as classical ethnography and media ethnography as methodological orientation. By working with exemplary and concrete cases, students will gain an initial understanding of how an analysis of use contexts can help improve existing products or make it possible to reach new user groups.Some examples of topics the course will cover (but are not limited to): the individual's motivation for using digital media products and servicesthe influence of technology on one's self-understanding (tracking and "the quantified self")domestication of technologiespower, agency and technology - how institutions and businesses try to influence our technology usehow users try to control their use of technology through disconnecting and disconnecting strategiesmedia-specific subculturesdiscussing the meaning of context in specific institutional contexts, such as the use of digital news services, the use of apps at cultural institutions and the use of digital technologies among children and young people in learning contextsglobal and cultural citizenship and counter-publicity as a context for activist use of network technologiesthe study of user behavior across media platformsdigital ethnography, netnography and media go-along as methods
Exam: C: Submission of written work, External (7-point scale)
Programme: MSc in Digital Design and Interactive Technologies

Course Summary: This course will enable students to understand, articulate, and work critically with values ​​and ethics in complex design contexts. Please note that this course will be offered in English in Autumn 2026
Abstract: This course will enable students to understand, articulate, and work critically with values ​​and ethics in complex design contexts. Please note that this course will be offered in English in Autumn 2026
Description: Design is an intentional change of the world and is therefore a deeply ethical and value-laden practice, whether we see it or not. The development of a responsible design practice, therefore, requires skills to bring ethical and value-based aspects of design into view. In this course, students will learn to incorporate ethics and values into their design and innovation processes. We will develop a theoretical lens, an analytical sensitivity, and a vocabulary that will enable students to work explicitly with values ​​and ethics in their design processes. The course will cover subjects such as situated ethics, care ethics, AI & ethics, values in design, and design ethos. The course will offer students an opportunity to strengthen a very central part of their design repertoire, an aspect that is increasingly crucial and a sought-after competence in the design and development of new technologies. Re GenAI: No use of generative artificial intelligence is allowed for the exam.
Exam: C: Submission of written work, Internal (7-point scale)
Programme: MSc in Digital Design and Interactive Technologies

Course Summary: Dette kursus vil sætte de studerende i stand til at forstå, artikulere og arbejde kritisk med værdier og etik i avancerede og komplekse design kontekster.
Abstract: Dette kursus vil sætte de studerende i stand til at forstå, artikulere og arbejde kritisk med værdier og etik i avancerede og komplekse design kontekster.
Description: I takt med at teknologi spiller en stadig større rolle i i både den professionelle og personlige personlige kontekst, vil de værdier og den etik hvormed vi designer teknologier blive stadig mere afgørende. Adgangen til personlige data, kunstige intelligenser og overvågning er tydelige eksempler. Bevidstgørelse, og evnen til at forstå, artikulere og arbejde med værdier og etik i design er en helt central design kompetence, og bliver i stigende en afgørende del af vores design repertoire. Nye teknologier vil åbne uendeligelige muligheder, og en afgørende diskurs i teknologidesign er derfor, ikke om vi kan, men om vi skal. Design er intentionel forandring af verden, og er derfor en dybt etisk og værdiladet praksis, hvad enten vi ser det eller ej. Udviklingen af en ansvarlig design praksis kræver derfor både indsigt, forståelse og metoder til kvalificeret at behandle de etiske og værdimæssige aspekter af design, både for den individuelle designer, teamet, organisationer og de lokale/globale kontekster vi designer til og for. På dette kursus vil de studerende lære at blive bevidst om hvordan man arbejder med etik og værdier i design og innovationsprocesser. Gennem både teoretiske reflektioner og praktiske værdi og etik fokuserede design metoder vil de studerende lære at tage ansvar for at se, arbejde med og artikulere hvilke værdier der træder i forgrunden i deres design proces. De studerende vil opbygge en forståelse af hvordan teknologier både forstærker og reducerer menneskers værdier og handlinger og derfor spiller en afgørende rolle for både sociale sammenhænge, social og miljømæssig bæredygtighed, virksomheder og demokrati. På kurset vil vi udarbejde både et ordforråd og metode katalog der vil gøre de studerende i stand til at arbejde eksplicit med værdier og etik i design processen, og i forskellige design kontekster, både kvalificeret og intentionelt. Kurset vil tilbyde de studerende en mulighed for at styrke en helt central del af deres design repertoire, et aspekt der både nu og i fremtiden vil være en efterspurgt kompetence i design og udvikling af nye teknologier.
Exam: C: Submission of written work, External (7-point scale)

Course Summary: Dette kursus vil sætte de studerende i stand til at forstå, artikulere og arbejde kritisk med værdier og etik i avancerede og komplekse design kontekster.
Abstract: Dette kursus vil sætte de studerende i stand til at forstå, artikulere og arbejde kritisk med værdier og etik i avancerede og komplekse design kontekster.
Description: I takt med at teknologi spiller en stadig større rolle i i både den professionelle og personlige kontekst, vil de værdier og den etik hvormed vi designer teknologier blive stadig mere afgørende. Adgangen til personlige data, kunstige intelligencer og overvågning er tydelige eksempler. Bevidstgørelse, og evnen til at forstå, artikulere og arbejde med værdier og etik i design er en helt central design kompetence, og bliver i stigende grad en afgørende del af vores design repertoire. Nye teknologier vil åbne uendelige muligheder, og en afgørende diskurs i teknologidesign er derfor, ikke om vi kan, men om vi skal. Design er intentionel forandring af verden, og er derfor en dybt etisk og værdiladet praksis, hvad enten vi ser det eller ej. Udviklingen af en ansvarlig design praksis kræver derfor både indsigt, forståelse og metoder til kvalificeret at behandle de etiske og værdimæssige aspekter af design, både for den individuelle designer, teamet, organisationer og de lokale/globale kontekster vi designer til og for. På dette kursus vil de studerende lære at blive bevidst om hvordan man arbejder med etik og værdier i design og innovationsprocesser. Gennem både teoretiske reflektioner og praktiske værdi og etik fokuserede design metoder vil de studerende lære at tage ansvar for at se, arbejde med og artikulere hvilke værdier der træder i forgrunden i deres design proces. De studerende vil opbygge en forståelse af hvordan teknologier både forstærker og reducerer menneskers værdier og handlinger og derfor spiller en afgørende rolle for både sociale sammenhænge, social og miljømæssig bæredygtighed, virksomheder og demokrati. På kurset vil vi udarbejde både et ordforråd og metode katalog der vil gøre de studerende i stand til at arbejde eksplicit med værdier og etik i design processen, og i forskellige design kontekster, både kvalificeret og intentionelt. Kurset vil tilbyde de studerende en mulighed for at styrke en helt central del af deres design repertoire, et aspekt der både nu og i fremtiden vil være en efterspurgt kompetence i design og udvikling af nye teknologier. Ingen brug af generativ kunstig intelligens er tilladt til eksamen.

Abstract: The goal of the course is to enable students to become better writers mastering a variety of text-genres - academic as well as commercial.
Description: Writing is an essential craft. Yet few, except professional writers, take the time to develop this skill. Writing clear, concise, and compelling arguments–knowing how to construct and tell a persuasive story–is crucial across industry and the digital world. Well-designed narratives can change the fortunes of a product, community, or company. This is a practice-based course that will provide students with a set of word crafting tools and an online studio space to explore how to write for the public, industry colleagues, executive management, and academic specialists. Students will gain experience in creative writing techniques and storytelling, along with tools for working with diverse empirical data. They will learn how to transform given research material and ideas into compelling texts in a variety of formats, from press releases and executive summaries, to podcasts and editorial blog posts. Emphasis is on written communication, but spoken and visual communication skills will also be included. Students will learn how to present and write for both conventional text, and a range of multimedia and digital platforms.

Abstract: Writing for Games is an introductory course that teaches students how to imagine, write and communicate characters, events and stories for games.
Description: Writing for Games is an introductory course that teaches students how to imagine, write and communicate characters, events and stories for games. The course aims at nurturing creative thinking and writing that leads to informed decisions regarding meaningful structure, order and type of game’s narrative elements. The course looks into how gameplay and game mechanics can work in harmony with game stories and support each other. Key areas of learning are game characters, story arcs and elements, pacing, plotting, dialogue, and branching. Use of generative artificial intelligence is allowed with restrictions during the exam (see LearnIT), as long as the student follows the official ITU guidelines on generative artificial intelligence.

Presenter: Assistant professor Marisa Cohn 3 May 2016 10.00 - 12.00 Room 3A07 (changed from 3A01) This TeachIT focuses on a cross-house topic: the teaching of computational competences. Computational competences are central to programs at ITU whether in developing programming skills learning to work with scripting languages for data analytics or understanding how algorithms shape our social and poltical landscape. This TeachIT aims to draw together these diverse approaches from across ITU programs to consider what various computational competences are currently being taught at ITU as well as what methods are available to us in our teaching. There is much discussion in Denmark and internationally about how to teach basic computational competences in higher education. But what is computational competence? We will begin by identifying and discussing the variety of computational approaches that are found in our current teaching at ITU. Selected researchers will present on their own approach to teaching computational competence in their courses. We will also ask participants to bring in one example from current teaching or idea for how one might teach computational competence. By sharing these we hope to gain an overview of the different approaches through which students are currently gaining computational competences as well as identify overlaps or gaps across these various approaches. This will also give us the chance to learn from each other what methods are available to us that we might adopt in our own teaching and consider new forms of teaching we might explore at ITU in the future. We will discuss: How do we teach computational competences? What are the computational skills desired and cultivated through different learning engagement formats? What different approaches to computational competence are there across various ITU programs? What overlaps or gaps are there across these various approaches? What methods might we adopt into our teaching that are appropriate for the learning objectives of different programs? In addition we will conclude with a brief discussion of how the teaching of computational competences intersects with concerns of interdisciplinarity and gender equity at the ITU. How does the approach to teaching computational competence meet the heterogeneous needs and expectations of our diverse student body? No preparation is required although participants will be invited to bring to the discussion an instance of how computational competence is taught in their courses. Course Name: teachIT - Teaching computational competencies - follow up
Course Summary: Teaching Computational Competencies - follow up 25 May 10.00 - 12.00 2A08 At the last TeachIT we discussed the topic of "computational competence" and what different meanings this takes on in the various fields and degree programs at ITU. This led to some engaged discussion of how we might understand computational competence through notions of depth abstraction and mastery and a consideration of the diverse forms of mastery we expect from our students. As a follow up to this TeachIT we will continue to discuss "computational competence" with a focus on the dimension of temporality and change in conversation with Visiting Professor Geof Bowker. An important aspect of teaching computational competence is to help our students gain skills in understanding and managing the continuous change and evolution of IT systems. At the same time the very skills that we might teach them are also evolving presenting challenges for how we maintain the relevance of our teaching to what students may encounter after obtaining their degrees. We will consider: how do we teach computational competence in the face of continuous change - when the very skills platforms languages and modes of governance of IT are continuously evolving? how do we teach our students to both understand and engage IT as a continuously evolving object and also prepare them for a world in which the skills that they require may also quickly obsolesce? Presenters Assistant professor Marisa Cohn Visiting Professor Geof Bowker Sign up We need to know who is coming so sign up no later than 24 May by sending an e-mail to learning consultant Mikkel Hvidtfeldt Andersen at hvma@itu.dk.

Multimodal teaching helps students to learn complex concepts because it allows to look at information from different perspectives. Engaging students with a game can be a useful mode of presenting information different from frontal lectures, Q&As, or peer group discussions. In this workshop, we present some theory behind the use of classroom games for teaching. We touch topics such as gamification, kinaesthetics, and perceivable consequences. We present examples we implemented in our teaching and will have you reason on how to introduce games in your own teaching.

me and date Monday 5 December from 14.00 - 16.00 Place: 2A08 The use of PowerPoint in presentation is extensive in modern universities and the benefit from this tool is obvious: It provides the presenter with the ability to distribute models photos and text in order to support the verbal presentation the slideshow can be produced in advance and saved afterwards the text is easier to read than writing on boards etc. However these advantages sometimes backfires for instance when the PowerPoint show controls the tempo and direction of the lecture when the information load becomes to massive and the written and spoken word competes for the students attention. Also quite often students tend to become more passive when PowerPoint shows are used too extensively partly because it often increases the one-way communication and partly because note taking becomes less important. In this workshop we will discuss how to use PowerPoint wisely and with the focus on student learning. The main topics will be: Pros and cons when using PowerPoint General guidelines for use of PowerPoint Illustrations and models in PowerPoint PowerPoint and timing PowerPoint and interaction The workshop consists of presentations discussions and exercises. Participant should bring their own laptop and a PowerPoint show they want to work with during the course. Intended Learning Outcomes After this workshop the participants should be able to Critically redesign their own slides based on general guidelines for use of PowerPoint Design slides with visual aids in order to enhance students learning outcome Use timing and the animation function in order to make more coherent presentations Use slides as tool for interaction in lectures Presenter Learning consultant Eva Ulstrup evul@itu.dk Sign up before 20 October 2016 to Kearning Consultant Mikkel Hvidtfeldt Andersen hvma@itu.dk

Course Name: teachIT: How to build a Research Seminar for students at ITU
Course Summary: "Although our ITU students turn out to be good engineers, ready for the industry after their studies, we see that they might come short with some skills that are vital for a scientifically valuable MSc thesis and a career in academia. These are: academic literature research, academic writing, and academic/science communication and presentation. So in this teachIT, I will present the concept of a Research Seminar that you can offer targeted at your field of research and integrated into a BSc/MSc course, potentially replacing the exercises part. Also, such a Research Seminar could be offered by a research group as a stand-alone module as an addition to the research projects."At this workshop you will learn:· Key components of the research seminar.· Particular content taught on reading, writing, and presenting, that is universal for academic research in IT and well compatible with constructive alignment.· Experiences from 10 years and >250 students of running research seminars.All three parts will be complemented with discussions within the teachIT workshop and take-home material for your own preparations.
